title: Captions Covered by Buttons? Fix Text Placement
description: Diagnose captions hidden by app controls, test long subtitle blocks, and improve placement in Reels, TikTok and Shorts.
body:
If subtitles look correct in your editor but disappear behind buttons after uploading, first check whether the problem is interface overlap or cropping. Interface overlap hides part of the picture beneath controls. Cropping removes part of the picture. Moving your caption can solve the first problem; the second may require changing your framing too.

This guide covers text you add to your video. Platform-generated captions are a separate layer and may behave differently.

Identify Which Layer Is Causing the Problem

Open the exported file outside the social app and pause at the affected line. If the full caption is already missing, return to the editing project. Check the text box, animation and export frame. A social safe-zone template will not repair text that was cut off during export.

If the exported caption is intact, compare the same moment inside the destination app. Note what covers it: the action buttons, account information, post description or another caption layer. Record the platform and viewing surface instead of assuming every viewer sees the same layout.

YouTube says automatic captions can contain transcription errors and should be reviewed. Fixing placement alone does not fix incorrect wording. YouTube automatic-caption guidance.

Test the Widest and Tallest Caption Blocks

Choose three moments: your longest line, your tallest wrapped caption and a line displayed during a busy shot. Short opening captions can pass while later lines reach into the right-side controls.

Open the comparison checker with your exported video. Pause at each moment and draw a manual region around the entire caption block, including its background. These regions are markers you position yourself; the checker does not automatically detect or track your subtitles.

Use the platform interface previews as planning aids. Review the current margins and adjust them when your own in-app preview shows different coverage. A passing result means your marked region clears the selected boundaries, not that every app layout has been tested.

Make the Smallest Useful Edit

Move a caption away from the obstruction before shrinking it. If the right-hand controls cover the end of a line, narrow the text block or rebreak the sentence. If the bottom metadata covers the second line, raise the whole block and check that it does not obscure a face or demonstration.

For example, suppose your marked caption ends at Y:1514 and your chosen planning boundary ends at Y:1500. That is 14 pixels of overlap in that scenario. Moving it upward by 38 pixels leaves 24 pixels of clearance. Those numbers illustrate the calculation; they are not a platform specification.

Apply the change in your editor. Moving a marker in the checker does not move the caption inside your video. Export a new file and repeat the check.

Check Readability While the Video Moves

A caption can fit inside the boundary and still be difficult to read. Play the whole sentence at normal speed on a phone-sized display. Check the background behind every word, not just the paused frame. Try a solid or partly opaque caption background when bright footage defeats the lettering.

Avoid crowding the same space with a hook, subtitles and a call to action. Show secondary messages at a different moment where possible. Keep the spoken message understandable with sound muted, and review names, numbers and punctuation manually.

Before You Publish

  • Confirm that the final exported file contains the revised captions.
  • Check the longest caption and every change in caption position.
  • Preview each destination separately, including any additional caption layer.
  • Keep an editable master so a platform-specific version is easy to make.

For a worked example, use the comparison tutorial. The measurement methodology explains why planning margins cannot guarantee identical results across devices.

If the words are in the right place but arrive at the wrong time, use the subtitle delay and drift guide. For a fresh placement check, return to the video safe zone checker.
h1: CAPTIONS COVERED by Buttons? Fix Text Placement

title: Reel Cover Text Cut Off? Check the Crop
description: Separate cover cropping from video overlays, test crop scenarios and keep your Reel cover headline readable at thumbnail size.
body:
A cover can look balanced at full size and lose its headline when shown as a smaller tile. Start by separating the cover image from the playing video. A crop preview answers which part of an image remains visible; a video safe-zone preview answers where interface elements may cover that image. You may need both checks.

Do not rebuild your cover around an unexplained pixel template. Establish which surface is failing and test a crop that matches what you actually see.

Compare the Original with the Affected Preview

Save your original cover and inspect it outside Instagram. Then compare it with the cover-selection preview and the affected surface in your account. Note whether the top, bottom or sides are missing, whether the image is repositioned, and whether the text is merely too small to read.

If the whole headline is visible but unreadable at tile size, cropping is not the main problem. Shorten the headline, simplify its background and enlarge the lettering. If part of a letter is missing, investigate the crop and placement first.

Account interfaces and viewing surfaces can differ. The scenarios below are geometry exercises, not claims that Instagram universally uses a particular crop today.

Understand What a Centered Crop Removes

Take a 1080 × 1920 image and keep its full width. A centered 4:5 crop has a height of 1350 pixels, so it removes 285 pixels from the top and 285 from the bottom. A centered 3:4 crop has a height of 1440 pixels, removing 240 pixels at each end. A centered square retains 1080 pixels of height and removes 420 pixels at each end.

These calculations assume a centered crop with no additional zoom. Repositioning changes which edges lose content. They explain why text close to the top of a tall image can disappear in a shorter preview without the original image being damaged.

In the crop previewer, use the available labelled scenario as a stress test. If it differs from your current Instagram preview, treat the in-app result as the relevant evidence and adjust the design accordingly. The tool does not reproduce every account's cover controls.

Build the Cover Around the Message

Put the essential headline and the identifying part of the subject near the center. Let decorative shapes and background detail extend toward the edges. Avoid making a border or line of text depend on a precise edge surviving.

Try a short headline such as “Three Lighting Fixes” instead of a sentence describing the entire video. That is an editorial choice, not an Instagram character limit. At tile size, check whether someone can identify the subject and read the headline without opening the image.

Save a separate cover version rather than editing the only copy. Compare the original and revised images in the same preview so you can tell whether your changes helped.

Recheck the Video Separately

A cover that survives a crop does not prove that subtitles in the video clear interface controls. Open the playing video in the Reels checker and inspect the hook, subtitles and final call to action. Keep cover checks and playback checks as separate steps in your publishing checklist.

If the Preview Still Looks Different

Verify that the intended cover file was selected and that you are comparing the same viewing surface. Keep a screenshot of the preview and record the date and device. Avoid repeatedly resizing from memory: the comparison should identify exactly what moved or disappeared.

CreatorSafeZone distinguishes mathematical crop scenarios from measured platform behavior. Read the evidence methodology before treating any template as a universal Instagram specification.

Use the crop planning tool for geometric scenarios. Use the Reels safe zone checker for controls over the full-screen video.
h1: REEL COVER Text Cut Off? Check the Crop

title: Create a Safe Zone Overlay in Canva
description: Create a reusable safe-zone overlay with a worked margin example, free transparent PNG and SVG downloads, and a practical Canva workflow.
body:
A safe-zone overlay is a temporary reference layer that helps you position text and logos while designing. It should match your video canvas, sit above your content during review and be removed before the final export.

Canva's ordinary margin guides are not a map of TikTok, Reels or Shorts controls. Canva describes margins and bleed primarily in its layout and print guidance, and documents rulers and guides separately. Canva's guide to margins and rulers.

Download the Worked-Example Overlay

Download the transparent PNG overlay or open the editable SVG source. Both use a 1080 × 1920 canvas with illustrative margins: top 180, right 180, bottom 360 and left 120 pixels. The clear working area is 780 × 1380 pixels, starting at X:120, Y:180.

These are teaching values, not measured or official platform boundaries. Red bands mark the example exclusions; the middle is transparent so your video can show through. Choose margins for your actual destination and preview. You may reuse and modify these original CreatorSafeZone guide files for personal or commercial editing.

Choose the Canvas and Planning Margins

Check the width and height of the design before importing a guide. A 1080 × 1920 guide has a 9:16 aspect ratio. A 720 × 1280 canvas has the same ratio, so uniform scaling can preserve the guide's proportions. A square canvas does not: stretching the guide to fit would change the relationship between its margins and the picture.

Use the guide for the actual delivery frame. If you are also creating a square or landscape version, treat that as another layout to review rather than stretching the vertical layout into shape.

Write down the four margins before drawing. For any canvas, working width equals canvas width minus left and right margins; working height equals canvas height minus top and bottom margins. For our example: 1080 − 120 − 180 = 780, and 1920 − 180 − 360 = 1380. If either result is zero or negative, reduce the margins or choose another canvas.

For ads, start with the reference for that specific ad format. For organic video, compare against the destination app's preview and label your template as a planning reference. Do not combine crop boundaries and interface coverage without explaining which each band represents.

Create the Overlay in Canva

Create a blank 1080 × 1920 design. Add four rectangles as guide bands, using these example positions measured from the top-left corner:

  • Top: X:0, Y:0, width 1080, height 180.
  • Bottom: X:0, Y:1560, width 1080, height 360.
  • Left: X:0, Y:180, width 120, height 1380.
  • Right: X:900, Y:180, width 180, height 1380.

The side bands stop at the top and bottom bands so their corners do not stack and become darker. Use a visible red fill with partial transparency. Leave the center empty; do not place a white rectangle over it. Put any labels inside the excluded bands so they do not obstruct the content you are checking.

Use your editor's available size and position controls to align the shapes. Canva documents desktop rulers and guides; availability and menu placement can vary. If precise positioning is difficult on your device, import our ready-made PNG instead of estimating the rectangle sizes by eye.

Save an editable copy, then choose PNG and the transparent-background export option if your Canva plan offers it. Canva lists transparent design downloads as a plan-dependent feature; the ready-made PNG above avoids needing that export feature just to obtain this example. Canva transparent-image information.

Check the downloaded image over a colored background. The middle should reveal the color underneath. A white middle means the export contains an opaque background; a JPG cannot preserve this transparency. Do not use a screenshot as a substitute for a transparent PNG.

Add the Guide as a Temporary Layer

From the comparison checker, choose the appropriate guide export for your workflow. Keep a note of its dimensions, platform or scenario, and selected margins. The exported guide reflects those settings; it is not an official platform approval.

Upload the guide image to your Canva design and position it over the full canvas. This is a manual transfer of an image file, not a connection that synchronizes the checker and Canva. Arrange the layer above the content you are checking. If your editor offers layer locking, lock it after alignment so you do not move it while adjusting text.

Before judging your captions, inspect the guide's alignment at all four edges. A guide that is offset, stretched or cropped can give misleading results even when its shaded regions look plausible.

Position the Complete Text Block

Keep the entire block inside your chosen working area, including its background shape and the ends of long lines. Leave some visual space from the boundary rather than aligning letters directly against it.

If moving the block covers your subject, shorten the message or change when it appears. Reducing every caption to tiny text can solve an overlap problem while creating a readability problem. Review the design at phone size after any substantial edit.

For a video with several scenes, inspect each scene and the longest caption. One carefully aligned opening frame says little about text that appears later. Repeat the review for each destination when their planning boundaries differ.

Remove the Guide and Verify the Export

Keep an editable copy containing the guide, then remove the reference layer from the version you intend to publish. Export the video and open the resulting file outside Canva. Look for leftover colored bands, border lines and labels, including at the end of the timeline.

Load the exported file back into the checker. This confirms you are reviewing the delivered picture rather than an earlier design state. Then inspect the destination app's own preview for account-specific controls and layout differences.

Common Problems

  • The overlay does not reach every edge: verify the canvas ratio and image sizing before changing the margins.
  • The text clears the overlay but is unreadable: review size, contrast, line breaks and on-screen duration.
  • The export contains the overlay: remove the reference layer from the publishing copy and export again.
  • The app still covers a label: revise the planning boundaries using the actual preview, then adjust the design.

Optional: Adapt the SVG in an Html Page

For a code-based workflow, use the downloadable SVG as an image over a video inside a shared 9:16 container. Give the image and video the same displayed bounds; keep the overlay from receiving pointer input so playback remains usable. Resizing only the video or using a different crop mode will misalign the guide.

The SVG source lists the rectangle coordinates from the worked example, so a developer can edit those numbers for another scenario. Embedding the SVG in HTML displays the guide; it does not automatically bake it into a video or create a Canva template. Use the PNG for the simplest Canva import, and remove all guide layers from the final creative.

For the next review step, follow the comparison-page tutorial.
h1: Create a SAFE ZONE OVERLAY in Canva

title: Organic vs Ad Safe Zones: Which Template Fits?
description: Choose the right ad safe-zone reference and review final captions and calls to action before handing off your video creative.
body:
Use an organic-video template as an early composition check, but verify an advertisement against its actual format and preview before delivery. An ad can introduce a call to action or other elements that your organic preview did not include. A familiar canvas size does not establish the usable area around those elements.

TikTok's in-feed ad documentation says the safe zone depends on dimensions, caption length and additional formats. It also provides different safe-zone files for ads using anchors. TikTok in-feed ad specifications.

Google likewise explains that overlays, calls to action and buttons can appear in different places depending on the ad format, campaign type and screen. Its video-ad specifications include reference templates. Google video-ad specifications.

Identify the Placement Before Editing

Write down the destination platform, selected ad format, canvas ratio, caption copy and planned call to action. If a colleague is setting up the campaign, ask for those details before you finalize text placement. “A vertical ad” is not enough information to choose a definitive overlay.

Download the current template from the relevant platform documentation when one is available. Keep the source link and access date with the project. Do not reuse a file merely because its filename contains the platform name; it may belong to a different format or older workflow.

Review the Parts That Must Remain Visible

Mark the product name, offer, logo and essential explanatory text. For each, ask whether an interface element can cover it and whether it stays readable against the moving background. If your design contains important qualifying information, include that in the layout review rather than treating it as expendable small text.

The vertical ad planning tool can help you explore an editable scenario. Its planning boundaries are not a replacement for campaign-specific requirements or a guarantee of platform approval. Set the boundaries to match your evidence and inspect the entire clip.

Compare the Final Copy and Call to Action

Test with the caption and call to action you intend to use. A layout checked with placeholder copy may behave differently when the real text is inserted. Keep enough room around the offer that an interface change does not immediately collide with it.

For example, an organic version might place its final instruction near the bottom. In the ad version, that instruction could compete with the platform's own call-to-action area. Move the instruction, change its timing or simplify the frame, then preview again. This is a design scenario, not a measured universal ad margin.

Use the Campaign Preview

Google documents a preview gallery and a YouTube preview option for supported Shorts video campaigns. Use the available preview for the campaign you are actually preparing. Google's Shorts preview instructions.

Check every placement included in your delivery plan. If one layout cannot serve them all, create separate versions with clear filenames. Keep the original editable project so the change is deliberate and repeatable.

Handoff Checklist

  • Record the intended format and the official reference used.
  • Check the final caption, call to action and any additional format elements.
  • Remove editing overlays before exporting.
  • Review the exported file and campaign preview.
  • Record unresolved differences instead of labelling an untested layout “approved.”

Safe placement is one part of ad preparation. It does not establish policy compliance, correct targeting or campaign performance. This guide addresses layout review only.
h1: Organic vs AD SAFE ZONES: Which Template Fits?

title: Black Bars or Cropped Faces? Check Fit and Fill
description: Find the cause of black bars and cropped faces by checking source footage, fit or fill scaling, canvas size and the exported file.
body:
When a vertical export has black bars or cuts off a face, compare three things: the source footage, the editing canvas and the exported file. They can have different dimensions. Selecting a vertical export preset does not necessarily repair a composition built for another frame.

Start with a short duplicate project so you can test changes without damaging your original edit.

Find Where the Mismatch Starts

Open the exported file in a regular video player and inspect its dimensions. If the file is landscape when you intended portrait, review the sequence and export settings. If the file is portrait but the picture occupies only a small area inside it, inspect how the source clip is scaled on the canvas.

Adobe's documentation shows that a sequence's horizontal and vertical frame dimensions determine its aspect ratio. Its separate image-sizing guidance describes scaling imported images to the sequence. These are different controls: the frame and the content inside it both matter. Sequence aspect ratio, imported-image sizing.

Also check whether the bars are already part of the source file. Scaling a picture that contains baked-in bars enlarges those bars too. Return to a clean source if you have one.

Choose What You Want to Preserve

Fit keeps the whole source picture inside the destination frame. When their ratios differ, space remains around it. You can use a deliberate background instead of leaving that space black.

Fill covers the destination frame while preserving the picture's proportions. Parts of the source extend beyond the edges and are cropped. This can work for a centered subject but can cut off a second speaker or a demonstration near the edge.

Stretching width and height independently avoids empty space by distorting the picture. Check faces, circles and product proportions before accepting a stretched result.

A Landscape-To-Portrait Example

Suppose a 1920 × 1080 landscape clip is fitted into a 1080 × 1920 portrait canvas. Scaling the clip to the canvas width gives a picture about 608 pixels tall. The remaining height needs a background or another intentional layout.

Filling the same portrait canvas scales the source to 1920 pixels tall, making it about 3413 pixels wide. Only 1080 pixels of that width remain visible. This explains why a fill operation can remove much of a landscape shot even though the output dimensions are correct.

These are geometric examples, not recommended crop coordinates. Choose the visible area around the content the viewer needs to understand.

Follow the Subject Through the Whole Clip

A crop that works at the opening may fail when someone moves sideways. Scrub through the timeline, especially cuts, gestures and demonstrations. Reposition the crop over time where your editor supports it, or use a fit layout when the full scene matters.

Check captions after reframing. Text baked into the source may be cropped along with the picture; editable text can be repositioned separately. If a subtitle disappears, determine which type you have before attempting a fix.

Verify the Actual Export

Export a short section containing the hardest shot. Confirm its dimensions and inspect it outside the editor. Once the framing is correct, load the final file into the comparison checker to review interface overlap separately.

CreatorSafeZone previews your media and planning regions; it does not reframe or re-export your video. Make the actual crop and scale changes in your editing project. Finish with each destination's preview, because a correctly framed file can still place text under app controls.
h1: BLACK BARS or Cropped Faces? Check Fit and Fill

title: Hard-to-Read Captions? Fix Size and Contrast
description: Troubleshoot small, low-contrast or rushed video captions with checks for moving backgrounds, phone-size playback and final placement.
body:
Captions can sit inside a safe area and still be difficult to read. If every word is visible but you struggle to follow the sentence, check the size of the lettering, its separation from the picture and how long it stays on screen. Moving the caption away from app buttons will not solve those problems by itself.

This guide focuses on captions burned into an exported video. Selectable caption tracks may give viewers their own display controls, so review those separately when your destination supports them.

Diagnose the Failure Before Changing the Style

Play a short section at normal speed on a phone-sized display. Avoid enlarging the preview to judge the text. Note what happens when you lose a word:

  • If letters merge into bright or detailed footage, investigate contrast.
  • If the caption is clear when enlarged but tiny at viewing size, investigate scale.
  • If you can read a paused frame but cannot finish the sentence during playback, investigate timing and text density.
  • If a button or description covers the words, use the separate caption placement guide.

Keep a copy of the original style and change one feature at a time. Comparing two short exports of the same scene is more useful than switching fonts throughout an entire project without checking the result.

Check the Background Throughout the Caption

Choose a caption that crosses a camera movement or scene change. Inspect the brightest and most detailed frames behind the words, not just the first frame. White lettering against a dark jacket may become difficult to distinguish when a window moves behind it.

Try a dark background box behind light text, leaving padding around the letters. An opaque box gives you a predictable local background; a translucent box still changes with the footage underneath. A shadow or outline can help, but check thin strokes and small gaps at the final display size rather than assuming the effect solves every frame.

W3C's WebVTT guidance explicitly calls for considering text color, background color and the video's color when evaluating caption contrast. WebVTT specification.

Use Contrast Measurements with the Right Context

WCAG's minimum contrast criterion uses 4.5:1 for ordinary text and 3:1 for qualifying large text, with defined exceptions. These are accessibility criteria, not social-platform safe-zone dimensions. Do not assume an editor's large font-size number qualifies the delivered caption as large text. W3C contrast explanation.

For a practical check, compare the intended text and background colors with a contrast checker. If the background is transparent, the box's fill color alone is not the resulting background: inspect the composite over your footage. A reading test remains useful even when the selected colors pass, because font weight, compression and motion can affect the delivered result. This workflow is not a complete accessibility audit.

Judge Size After the Video Is Scaled Down

There is no single editor font-size setting that establishes readability across every font and viewing size. As a geometric example, a 60-pixel-high element in a 1080-pixel-wide frame becomes about 20 pixels high when the whole frame is displayed 360 pixels wide. That calculation explains scaling; it is not a recommended caption size or a measurement of glyph height.

Use a simple, clearly drawn typeface and inspect the actual letters. If increasing the size produces an overly wide block, adjust the line breaks before shrinking everything again. Keep each line understandable, and check that descenders and accents remain inside the caption background.

Review Timing Without Removing Meaning

Watch with sound muted and see whether you can finish each caption before it changes. Ask someone unfamiliar with the video to try the same passage if possible. Your own familiarity can make a rushed sentence seem easier than it is.

If the passage is too dense, consider slowing the edit or dividing the caption at meaningful points. Do not silently remove necessary dialogue merely to make the styling look cleaner. Check the transcript and synchronization as separate tasks from visual design.

Recheck Placement After Improving Readability

A larger font or background box occupies more space. Load the revised export into the comparison checker, mark the entire caption block and inspect it against your selected planning margins. The checker evaluates manually marked regions; it does not measure contrast, read your subtitles or certify accessibility.

Finish by reviewing the exported file and the destination app preview. Keep the successful style as a starting point for later videos, but retest it when the background, framing or caption length changes.

If reading is difficult because the caption arrives too early or late, diagnose subtitle timing drift or a fixed delay before changing type size.
h1: HARD-TO-READ CAPTIONS? Fix Size and Contrast

title: Burned-In vs Closed Captions: Avoid Double Subtitles
description: Choose caption layers, diagnose double subtitles and check the final viewing experience without losing useful caption information.
body:
Two sets of subtitles can compete for the same space: one exported inside your video and another drawn by the viewing app. Before moving text higher, identify which layer you can actually edit. A placement change cannot remove words already embedded in the picture.

This guide helps you choose a caption delivery workflow and review the final viewing experience. It does not assume that every social platform accepts a separate subtitle file or exposes the same caption controls.

Identify the Caption Layers

Open the exported video in a local player with subtitle tracks disabled. If the words remain visible, they are burned into the picture. If they disappear, they were supplied by a separate track or player feature. Also check whether your editor exported a subtitle file beside the video.

W3C distinguishes open captions from closed captions: open captions remain visible, while closed captions can be switched on and off. Captions should convey relevant speech and sounds; decorative headlines alone are not a replacement. A burned-in transcript with missing words can still leave viewers without the information they need.

Choose the Workflow Before the Final Export

Use burned-in captions when you need a specific visual treatment to travel with the video. You control their position in the exported picture, but correcting a typo requires another video export. Keep the editable project so this correction is practical.

Use a separate caption track where the destination supports it and viewer control matters. Review that destination's current upload options rather than assuming an SRT file can be attached everywhere. The viewing app may determine the appearance and position, so an editor screenshot cannot confirm the final layout.

For a reusable project, keep a clean video export and a captioned version with clear filenames. For example, use “launch-clean-v2” and “launch-captioned-v2” alongside the matching subtitle file. This is an organizational suggestion, not a required platform naming convention.

Diagnose Double Captions Without Removing Access

  1. Play the actual export locally and note which text is permanent.
  2. Inspect the destination's upload preview and available caption settings.
  3. Check whether automatic captions or an uploaded track add another visible layer.
  4. Review both captions-on and captions-off states where the player permits them.
  5. Choose the appropriate export and caption setup, then repeat the check.

Do not automatically delete the accessible track just to tidy a screenshot. First consider whether a clean video with a reviewed caption track meets the publishing need. If you retain burned-in text and a separate track, assess the combined viewing state and the information available when either layer is absent.

Check Placement Separately from Delivery

Load the captioned export into the multi-platform checker. Pause on the longest line, a speaker change and the final call to action. Mark the full caption block, including its background panel, rather than just the central words.

The checker helps compare your exported composition with its configured guide regions. It does not import subtitle tracks or reproduce every viewer's caption settings. Follow the caption obstruction guide if app buttons cover the permanent text, then verify the real destination preview.

Final Handoff Checklist

Record which video version is intended for each destination and whether a separate caption file is required. Check spelling, speaker names, meaningful sounds and timing. Watch with sound off to see whether the message still makes sense, then watch with sound to catch mismatched words. Keep the clean master and editable captions together so future revisions do not require rebuilding the entire project.
h1: BURNED-IN VS CLOSED CAPTIONS: Avoid Double Subtitles

title: Premiere Pro Safe Margins and Social Overlays
description: Use Premiere margins alongside a temporary social video overlay, check moving text and verify the final export.
body:
Premiere's Safe Margins are useful composition guides, but a generic inset does not describe every social app's buttons, account information or expanded description. For vertical video, treat editor margins as one review aid and check the intended viewing layout separately.

This workflow is for an existing vertical edit. It helps you keep a temporary overlay aligned, review changing captions and remove the guide before delivery. It does not claim that one rectangle guarantees visibility across devices or placements.

Start with the Correct Sequence

Confirm that the sequence matches the intended deliverable before positioning text. A 1080 × 1920 example overlay belongs on a matching 9:16 canvas. If your project uses another size or aspect ratio, adapt the guide deliberately rather than stretching it until it looks close.

Check the footage's scale and crop independently. A correctly aligned overlay cannot repair a face already cropped by a fill operation. Resolve those framing choices first so later caption adjustments refer to the final composition.

Understand What Safe Margins Show

Adobe documents Safe Margins in the Source and Program monitors. Enable them from the monitor's available settings or panel menu when you need an editor reference. The controls may vary with your version and workspace.

Do not infer a specific TikTok, Reels or Shorts interface from a generic margin guide. If you use a platform template or preset, inspect what it represents, who supplied it and which viewing state it covers. A template name alone is not evidence that it matches the placement you are publishing to.

Add a Temporary Overlay Track

Use a transparent PNG guide whose canvas dimensions match your sequence. The custom overlay tutorial includes an editable example and explains its custom margins. That example is a planning aid, not an official platform specification.

Import the image and place it on a dedicated video track above the edit. Align the complete image with the sequence frame; avoid a crop or transform that shifts its edges. Extend its duration over the section you want to inspect, and label the track clearly so another editor understands why it exists.

Keep the guide separate from the footage and text. This makes it easier to hide while judging visual quality and to remove before export. If the guide seems to move, check whether you transformed a nest or parent composition rather than only the footage beneath it.

Review More Than the Opening Frame

Pause at the longest caption, a two-line speaker exchange, any animated headline and the closing call to action. Watch the motion between these points as well: a title can start inside a guide and travel outside it during its animation.

Review the full text panel, not only its baseline. Background shapes, shadows and labels can occupy space beyond the letters. If a scene is crowded, shorten or reposition the text before reducing its size until it becomes difficult to read.

Export and Verify the Delivered File

Hide or remove the temporary overlay track before exporting. Open the resulting video and confirm that no guide lines remain. Also confirm the dimensions and that captions belong to the correct revision.

Then load the export into the comparison checker to compare its composition with the configured platform regions. Finish in the destination's own preview for the intended placement. Neither the editor's margins nor a browser simulation substitutes for that final check, especially when descriptions or interface controls change.

For a repeatable editing brief, follow the comparison and editor handoff checklist.
h1: Premiere Pro SAFE MARGINS and Social Overlays

title: Video Not Playing? Check the File and Codec
description: Troubleshoot local video files, codecs, direct URLs and cross-origin access in the CreatorSafeZone preview.
body:
If a video will not load in CreatorSafeZone, first separate a file problem from a link problem. Try the saved video through Choose a file. If that works but the URL fails, changing safe-zone margins will not help: the browser is having trouble obtaining the remote media.

The checker previews supported video files. It is not a social-video downloader or a live-stream player. The following checks help you choose a usable source without changing your video's layout unnecessarily.

Start with a Small Local Export

Choose an MP4 or WebM video from your device. The current checker limits selected files to 250 MB and uses the file's reported media type when deciding whether to accept it. A renamed extension does not convert the video or repair an unsupported type.

If a large export fails, make a short test copy in your editor. Keep the original project and master file. A smaller copy is easier to retry and helps establish whether the problem affects the whole recording or just a particular export.

Local selections are processed in your browser by the checker. Choosing a remote URL instead contacts that media host. You do not need to put a private client video on a public server merely to inspect its composition.

Check the Codec Inside the File

MP4 describes a container, not a guarantee that every browser can decode its contents. MDN's codec guide identifies MP4 with H.264 video and AAC audio as a broadly supported combination. Device capabilities and the particular export still matter.

If the original file fails, try a new H.264 MP4 export from your editor and select it locally. Do not simply rename a MOV file to MP4. Confirm that the new file opens and has the expected duration before returning to the checker.

Use a Direct Media Link

A social post URL or cloud-storage sharing page usually opens a webpage, not the video file itself. The URL option needs a direct playable video resource. A link can also stop working when its access token expires or the host requires a signed-in session.

Opening a URL in another tab is a useful clue, but successful playback there does not prove that another website can use it. If you have permission to use the video, choosing the saved file is often the simplest way to separate remote-access problems from decoding problems.

Understand Cross-Origin Restrictions

CreatorSafeZone requests remote videos with anonymous cross-origin access. The source host must permit that access; a video can fail here even though its own website plays it. MDN explains the crossorigin setting and how it affects media requests.

If you control the host, have its owner check the media response and cross-origin configuration. Otherwise, use an authorized local copy. Do not disable browser security or send private media through an unknown proxy to bypass the restriction.

Distinguish Live Streams from Video Files

HLS and DASH playlist links, commonly ending in .m3u8 or .mpd, are not supported by this checker. For a live production, export a representative recording segment and inspect that file. The result only describes that segment and the selected guide settings.

Once playback works, open the multi-platform checker, pause on important frames and mark the content you want to assess. If the video plays but shows unwanted bars or cropping, continue with the fit and fill guide; that is a separate composition problem.

Once playback works, return to the main video checker and mark the complete elements you want to inspect.
h1: VIDEO NOT PLAYING? Check the File and Codec

title: Subtitles Out of Sync? Fix Delay and Drift
description: Diagnose fixed caption delays, timing drift and mismatched edits before checking subtitle placement.
body:
When captions appear before or after speech, moving them higher on the screen will not solve the problem. First establish whether every caption is displaced by the same amount, whether the error grows over time, or whether only one section is wrong.

Work with a copy of the subtitle file or an editable caption track. Keep the final video beside it and give both matching revision names. Timing against an older cut is a common way to fix one section while making another worse.

Compare Three Points in the Final Video

Choose a clear spoken word near the beginning, middle and end. Note when it is heard and when its caption appears. Use normal-speed playback as well as the editor's timeline; a still frame cannot show whether viewers have enough time to read the line.

For example, if the first, middle and final captions all arrive about 0.8 seconds late, a shared offset may be appropriate. If the first line is correct but the last arrives several seconds late, investigate drift or a mismatched edit instead. These numbers illustrate a diagnosis, not a recommended reading duration.

Correct a Fixed Offset Carefully

Use your caption editor's timing adjustment to shift the affected cues together. Late captions need to move earlier; early captions need to move later. For a cue that starts at 12.0 seconds and is 0.8 seconds late, the illustrative corrected start is 11.2 seconds.

Shift the end time by the same amount when preserving the cue's duration. Check cues near the beginning so they do not move before the video starts. Recheck the three sample points after the adjustment, and watch the surrounding dialogue rather than relying on the arithmetic alone.

Investigate Drift Before Changing Everything

Confirm that the subtitle file belongs to the final export. Look for a trimmed introduction, inserted scene, removed pause or speed change. An error that begins immediately after one edit may require retiming only the later section, rather than stretching the entire track.

Do not change the video's frame rate merely because an online example mentions it. First compare the actual edit and caption timeline. If timing errors vary irregularly, reviewing individual cues or regenerating captions from the final audio may be more reliable than applying one global adjustment.

Use the destination's Timing Tools Where Available

YouTube documents editing caption timestamps in its captions editor, including an Edit timings option when timestamps are hidden. It also describes downloading caption files for editing and uploading the revised result. Follow the current interface for your account and selected language track.

Other destinations may provide different controls or accept different file types. Keep the editable subtitle source even if you eventually burn the words into the picture. Once captions are embedded in the video, changing their timing normally means exporting the video again from the project.

Finish with Timing and Placement Checks

Watch the entire corrected result, paying attention to speaker changes, short interjections and the final sentence. Check that cues do not linger over unrelated speech and that important sound information has not disappeared during editing. Confirm the correct caption track is selected in the viewing app.

CreatorSafeZone does not import or retime SRT files. After correcting timing in your editor, use a captioned video export in the comparison checker to assess placement. If the words are synchronized but hidden by controls, use the separate caption placement guide. Timing and visibility both need to work for the final viewer.

After correcting timing, check caption readability and use the placement checker to review the final export.
h1: SUBTITLES OUT OF SYNC? Fix Delay and Drift

title: DaVinci Resolve Safe-Zone Overlay Workflow
description: Add a temporary guide track in Resolve, check moving captions and disable the overlay before rendering your final vertical video.
body:
To check a social-video layout in DaVinci Resolve, place a matching transparent guide on a separate track above your edit, inspect the full sequence, then disable that track before rendering. A guide helps you compose; it does not move captions or promise that every app interface will leave them visible.

You can do this with a still PNG. A plugin is optional. The important choices are the guide's canvas, the timeline it represents and how you keep it out of the delivered video.

Prepare the Timeline and Guide

Confirm the timeline's dimensions before importing the overlay. For a 1080 × 1920 project, use a guide with the same canvas and intended orientation. A landscape recording-monitor overlay may contain a portrait rectangle inside a wider image; that is different from a full-frame portrait editing guide.

Open the custom overlay tutorial if you need an example PNG or want to define your own margins. The supplied example uses illustrative custom values. Treat third-party platform presets as references with a date and stated scope, rather than measured facts about your audience's devices.

Put the PNG Above the Edit

Import the guide into the Media Pool and place it on a dedicated video track above the footage and titles you want to inspect. Extend the still over the relevant sequence. Give the track a clear name such as “GUIDE — disable before render” and keep it separate from graphics intended for delivery.

Check the image's alignment against all four frame edges. If the guide is unexpectedly cropped or offset, inspect its scale and position rather than moving your captions to compensate. Avoid applying the footage's creative zoom or stabilization to the guide itself.

Blackmagic's official Resolve training includes editing and delivery lessons. Use the guide matching your installed version for interface details. This workflow does not depend on a particular paid effect or assume that a generic title-safe marker reproduces a social platform's controls.

Review Changing Content

Inspect the longest caption, a speaker label, a moving title and the closing call to action. Play between these moments too. A title's resting position can fit while its entrance animation crosses a guide boundary.

If a caption background extends beyond the words, assess the whole panel. Review scenes where a face or product moves behind that panel. Shortening a line or adjusting its timing can preserve more of the picture than repeatedly making the font smaller.

Toggle the guide off periodically to judge the actual composition. The overlay's color and shading can conceal low contrast or make a crowded frame feel more organized than the clean export really is.

Render Without the Temporary Track

Disable or remove the guide track before starting the final render. Check the render range and output dimensions, then open the resulting file independently of the project. Inspect several points for stray guide lines, missing captions and an incorrect revision.

Load that export into the comparison checker and mark the important content to compare it with the configured planning regions. Finish in the intended destination's own preview. Keep the guide file and its settings with your editable project so another editor can repeat the review without guessing which rectangle you used.

title: Transparent PNG Looks Black? Check Alpha and Layers
h1: TRANSPARENT PNG Looks Black? Check the Overlay
description: Diagnose an opaque PNG overlay by testing alpha, layer order and export choice before changing blend modes in your video editor.
body:
A black background behind a PNG does not by itself prove that transparency is missing. The viewer may be showing transparent pixels against black, or the image may contain an actual opaque rectangle. Place it over a bright test background in your editor to tell the difference before changing blend modes.

This distinction matters when importing a safe-zone guide: the center should let you see the footage underneath, while the guide marks remain visible.

Test the File Over Two Backgrounds

Place the PNG above a solid light background, then try a colored background. If the open area reveals both backgrounds, transparency is working. If the same black or white rectangle remains, inspect the image itself and how the editor interprets it.

A checkerboard shown in an image editor usually represents transparency, but a screenshot of that checkerboard contains ordinary image pixels. Download the original asset rather than taking a screenshot of a preview or saving a thumbnail from a results page.

Check Alpha, Not Just the Extension

MDN's image-format reference documents PNG's alpha transparency support. Alpha describes how transparent or opaque a pixel is. A PNG can support transparency and still contain only opaque pixels; the extension alone cannot tell you which you have.

Return to the editable design and hide any solid background layer. Export a PNG using that application's transparency option, where available, then repeat the two-background test. Renaming a JPEG to PNG cannot restore transparency that was never saved. If an export option is unavailable in your current account or editor, use another authorized workflow that preserves alpha rather than assuming the file will be transparent.

Check the Editor's Layer Stack

Keep the PNG on a track above the footage. If no clip or background lies underneath it, the editor can legitimately show black through the transparent region. That is empty composition space, not necessarily a black box stored in the image.

Temporarily disable effects on the image and use the editor's normal compositing behavior. If the source has a working alpha channel, special blend modes should not be your first repair. A Screen blend can hide black pixels while also changing the guide's dark marks and colors, making the result harder to evaluate.

When transparency works but a fringe remains around the edges, inspect the source at normal size and review the editor's alpha-interpretation settings. Avoid random changes across the entire project. The correct setting depends on how that particular asset was exported.

Choose the Correct CreatorSafeZone Export

The checker offers different outputs for different jobs. Use the transparent guide PNG when you need a temporary editing layer. A comparison image contains the preview composition and is intended for review or handoff. It is not the same asset as an empty guide.

For a reusable example and alignment steps, see the custom safe-zone overlay tutorial. Match the guide's full canvas to the project before adjusting text. Keep intentional translucent shading separate from an unexpected opaque center.

Once the overlay behaves correctly, review the video, disable the guide and export a short test. Open that test to verify the guide is absent. If the file is still opaque in multiple editors, replace or regenerate the asset from its editable source instead of repeatedly re-encoding your video.

title: Blurry Captions After Export? Find the Softening Step
h1: BLURRY CAPTIONS After Export? Check These Steps
description: Compare the editor preview, saved export and uploaded playback to find why captions look blurry and choose a focused correction.
body:
Find the first stage where the captions become soft: the editor preview, the saved video or the uploaded playback. Comparing those stages is more useful than repeatedly increasing every quality setting. Keep the original project and make a short test export containing the affected text.

This guide concerns visible detail in the rendered words. If the words are sharp but difficult to read over the footage, use the separate caption readability guide.

Compare at a Useful Viewing Size

Open the saved export in a local player and pause on the same caption you inspected in the editor. Check at normal viewing size and, when investigating pixels, at a one-to-one display scale. Filling a much larger monitor with a smaller video enlarges its pixels; that alone does not identify a faulty export.

Also inspect the editor's preview-quality setting. A reduced-resolution preview can look soft even when the final render is acceptable. Judge the actual exported file before changing a caption style that already works.

Separate Text Problems from Whole-Frame Problems

If the footage and captions both lose detail, compare the project's dimensions with the export dimensions. Check whether you accidentally exported a smaller version or reused a compressed copy. CapCut's official blurry-video troubleshooting identifies source quality and export settings as relevant checks; its controls are specific to that editor.

If only the captions are soft, identify whether they are editable text or imported graphics. A small caption image enlarged inside the editor has limited source detail. Recreate it at an appropriate size or return to editable text rather than exporting the same small image at a higher video resolution.

For an illustrative case, stretching a 540-pixel-wide full-frame graphic to 1080 pixels doubles its width. The larger output cannot recover letter detail missing from that source. This calculation describes scaling, not a universal caption-size recommendation.

Change One Export Variable at a Time

Keep the same short section and compare two exports. Start with the intended dimensions and an appropriate quality preset for your editor. If you investigate compression, hold dimensions and caption styling steady so you can see what changed.

Avoid cycling through social downloads, messaging-app copies and fresh exports as if they were equivalent masters. Name the tests clearly and compare them with the original project. A sharpening effect may alter edges, but it cannot reconstruct detail lost in a tiny source graphic or a severely reduced export.

Check Uploaded Playback Separately

If the local file is clear and the uploaded version is soft, check the destination's available playback quality and whether processing has finished. Compare the same timestamp. Do not assume that a single low-quality preview proves the file itself is defective, or that a particular bitrate will prevent every platform from processing it.

Keep a record of which export you uploaded. Otherwise, it is easy to assess an earlier test while changing the newest project.

Finish with a Placement Review

After resolving the rendering problem, inspect the captions at phone size over moving footage. Load the final captioned export into the comparison checker to review the marked text block against its planning regions. The checker does not measure sharpness or improve video quality. It helps catch the separate problem of a clear caption sitting beneath interface controls.

title: Video Plays Sideways? Fix Rotation Before Placement
h1: VIDEO PLAYS SIDEWAYS? Fix Rotation First
description: Separate display rotation from cropping, correct the clip in your editor and test an upright export before positioning captions.
body:
If a clip is upright on your phone but sideways in an editor or preview, investigate orientation before changing the canvas or cropping. The file may contain display-rotation information that different software handles differently. A quarter-turn correction and a portrait crop solve different problems.

Keep the original recording. Make changes in a copy of the project so you can compare the correction without losing the source or repeatedly compressing an already exported file.

Compare the Original in Two Places

Open the original clip in a player and in the editor. Note whether the whole image is sideways, only the frame is the wrong shape, or text appears mirrored. A sideways face suggests rotation; an upright person with unwanted bars suggests a framing decision. Reversed lettering suggests a mirror operation and needs a different correction.

Record the file you tested rather than relying on a screenshot from an earlier export. If the footage and captions were combined at different stages, the picture can be rotated while the words remain upright, or the reverse.

Understand Metadata and Rendered Rotation

Rotation can be represented as display information without changing the encoded picture in the same way as a new render. FFmpeg's documentation distinguishes display-rotation metadata from rotation applied during transcoding and documents its automatic-rotation behavior. That distinction explains why inspecting only the width and height may not explain what a player displays.

A rotation correction rendered into a new video changes the picture itself. Exporting that correction can introduce another compression pass, so work from the original and preserve a good master. Do not add a manual turn merely because a file inspector reports landscape dimensions if the editor already displays the clip correctly.

Correct the Clip Before Adding Captions

In your editor, rotate the clip only as needed to make its contents upright. Use a visible reference such as a door frame, face or readable sign. Then choose the intended output canvas and adjust the framing.

For an illustrative quarter-turn of a 1920 × 1080 picture, the corresponding rotated picture is 1080 × 1920 before any additional scaling or padding. Your editor may retain its existing project canvas, so verify the actual export dimensions instead of assuming the timeline changed with the clip.

Add or reposition captions after this correction. Rotating a finished composition can turn the text with the image, while rotating only the background clip can leave titles in their original orientation. Review the relationship deliberately rather than moving each element by trial and error.

Export a Short Orientation Test

Render a few seconds and open the result outside the project. Check the face or reference object, readable text and output frame. Load the same test in the destination preview you intend to use. If it turns again, investigate the export's orientation handling before repeating the rotation; another quarter turn can make a correct project wrong.

If the corrected picture is upright but bars or cropping remain, follow the fit and fill guide. Once the composition is settled, inspect the export in the comparison checker. CreatorSafeZone previews the file as the browser decodes it; it does not rotate or re-encode the original recording for you.

title: Translated Subtitles Too Long? Fix the Layout
h1: TRANSLATED SUBTITLES Too Long? Fix the Layout
description: Review translated subtitles for meaning, line breaks, timing and script rendering, then test each language version for placement.
body:
A translation can need different line breaks, more screen space or more reading time than the original caption. Review each language as its own timed layout. Reusing the source caption's rectangle and making the translated font smaller can leave the words technically visible but difficult to follow.

Start with a corrected source transcript and the final video cut. Keep separate, clearly named subtitle files or project versions for each language so an edit to one does not silently overwrite another.

Check Meaning Before Fitting the Box

Have a fluent reviewer check the translation in context, including names, references, negation and speaker changes. Automatic translation can provide a draft, but fitting that draft on screen does not establish that it conveys the right message.

If the words must be shortened, preserve the meaning and the important audio information. Do not remove a qualifying word or speaker label simply to recover a few pixels. Record approved terminology when a series repeats the same product, person or technical phrase.

Rebuild Line Breaks for the Target Language

Read the complete sentence before dividing it. Keep meaningful word groups together where the target language allows it, and review the actual rendered result rather than only a character counter.

Netflix's general timed-text guide provides examples of grammatical units to preserve across line breaks. Those are Netflix delivery requirements and editorial examples, not universal social-platform dimensions. A character limit from one language or delivery specification does not define how every font and script will occupy a portrait frame.

For a hypothetical English example, “Keep the original file / before making changes” preserves two useful phrases. Breaking after “the” would separate it from “original file.” Apply the equivalent grammatical judgment in the translated language rather than mechanically copying the English break.

Balance Space and Reading Time

If the translation becomes too dense, first review the wording and line breaks. Consider separate sequential cues where the speech and available timing permit them. Splitting one crowded cue into two very brief flashes does not automatically make it readable.

Play the result at normal speed with the picture. Check whether a viewer can read the caption while following the action, especially around cuts or demonstrations. If you change cue times, recheck synchronization against the final audio and use the subtitle timing guide when the problem is an offset or drift.

Inspect the Script in the Actual Renderer

Confirm that your selected font includes the characters you need. Look for missing-glyph boxes, clipped accent marks, unexpected word joining and punctuation in the wrong visual position. Right-to-left text mixed with numbers or Latin names needs review in the editor and final viewing environment; a plain-text document alone cannot establish the result.

If subtitles are delivered as a separate track, the destination may control their appearance. If they are burned into the picture, check the exported video. Keep this delivery choice explicit when handing files to another editor.

Review Each Language's Placement

Export a captioned sample for each version and load it into the comparison checker. Mark the entire translated block, including its background. A source-language layout that fit previously does not establish that the translated block fits too.

CreatorSafeZone does not translate or import subtitle files. Use it for the visual placement step after language and timing review, then confirm the intended destination preview. Keep the approved translation, timing file and matching video revision together for future corrections.

title: Vertical Screen Recordings: Keep Tutorial Text Readable
h1: VERTICAL SCREEN RECORDING: Keep UI Text Readable
description: Plan readable vertical screen tutorials around each control and its result. Check capture area, crop movement, captions and the final export.
body:
Frame each tutorial step around the control viewers must read and the result they need to notice. A portrait canvas alone cannot make a wide desktop interface readable on a phone. Plan the visible area before recording, then check every menu, click and confirmation in the exported video.

You can use your existing recorder and editor for this review. The goal is a sequence someone can follow without enlarging the video to discover which button you selected.

Choose the Smallest Useful Capture Area

Rehearse the action once and note which panels it uses. If everything happens in one application window, recording that window can give you a cleaner starting point than including unrelated desktop space. If the action opens a separate dialog, check that your chosen capture method includes it.

For example, Microsoft's Clipchamp recording guidance describes whole-screen, application-window and browser-tab choices for its work-account workflow. The options available in your recorder may differ. Test the resulting recording rather than assuming every pop-up belongs to the captured surface.

Before capturing, enlarge the application's text where appropriate and arrange the panels you actually need. If narrowing a window changes its layout, rehearse that version too. Use clean demonstration content so personal messages or file details do not become part of the lesson.

Pair the Action with Its Result

Build a short list of what the viewer must see at each stage. This hypothetical export lesson illustrates the check:

Event Keep Visible
Open the export menu The menu label and the option selected
Choose an output format The format name and the setting that changed
Finish the export The completion message or resulting file

A crop can show the pointer perfectly while excluding the menu item it selects. Likewise, a zoom that arrives after the click can hide the explanation. Review the moment before the action, the selection itself and the resulting state.

If these elements cannot fit clearly together, separate the lesson into closer views with enough context to understand the transition. Keep the camera movement purposeful; a moving pointer does not mean the frame must chase every movement.

Crop for Understanding, Then Check the Edges

Choose the intended canvas in your editor and decide which interface area belongs in each shot. Microsoft's cropping documentation distinguishes setting the visible area from filling the project frame. Filling the frame can remove content near its edges, so inspect the actual controls after that change.

For general scaling and border diagnosis, use the fit and fill guide. Here, the extra requirement is continuity: the viewer needs to connect the control you used with its outcome.

If the full interface must remain visible, consider a brief overview followed by a closer view of the active panel. Avoid shrinking a dense dashboard until every label fits but none can be read.

Check Captions and the Actual Export

Keep your caption block clear of the control being demonstrated, including menus that appear later. Export a short section containing the hardest interaction and watch it at phone size and normal speed. Try identifying the selected control from the video alone.

If the local export is soft despite an appropriate layout, investigate the rendering stage separately. Changing the crop repeatedly is not a substitute for diagnosing export quality.

Finally, load the export into the comparison checker. Mark the important label, active panel or caption block to review it against the configured planning regions. The checker evaluates your marked rectangles; it does not read interface text, verify tutorial accuracy or edit the recording. Confirm the intended destination preview after applying changes in your editor.
